title: Rereading chapters 1–4
hook: reread the twin verses, earnestness, thought, flowers
tomorrow: the old verses have a fool and a wise one. which one is you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pingiya's devotion: an old man who couldn't follow on foot. I follow in mind. And the far shore, read through. Now, what do old pages say when you come back changed?
screen: `I FOLLOW IN MIND.` → `WHAT DO OLD PAGES SAY NOW?`

segments.voice: A song from years ago comes on in the grocery store, and a line you sang over and over suddenly means something, because now you've lived it. The words didn't change. You did. That's today: back to the Dhammapada, the old book of the Buddha's verses, chapters one to four: the twin verses, earnestness, thought and flowers. Same pages, after two weeks on the far shore. Different reader. So what jumps out this time that didn't before?
screen: `A SONG IN THE GROCERY STORE.` → `THE WORDS DIDN'T CHANGE.` → `SAME PAGES, DIFFERENT READER.`

segments.voice: Open to the first verse, in Max Müller's translation: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." After weeks of poems about views, that line lands differently. The teachers in the square, each calling theirs true, were made up of their thoughts too. Turn to chapter two, earnestness: "Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death." And a few verses on, something that wasn't there before, or was and waited: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm." An island, and a flood. Kappa asked for exactly that, and now the old verse answers back. Chapter three compares the wavering mind to an arrow a fletcher straightens. Chapter four, flowers, says fine words that aren't lived are like a bright flower with no scent. That's rereading: new verses in old pages. And look how this fortnight gathers: cross yourself, what I rely on, the island, stilled, look on it as empty, I follow in mind. Each one makes an old line a little louder, the way a friend's voice is easier to pick out once you know it. The pages wait. The reader comes back changed.
screen: `ALL THAT WE ARE: OUR THOUGHTS.` · `EARNESTNESS, THE PATH.` · `AN ISLAND NO FLOOD CAN OVERWHELM.` · `A FLOWER WITH NO SCENT.` · then, large: `NEW VERSES IN OLD PAGES.`

segments.voice: If there's paper nearby, copy one line from today by hand, the one that caught you, slowly, in your own writing. Then read it back once, as if someone else had written it for you. Ask what it says to the person you are this week, and sit with that, breathing easily, until the bell.
Rereading chapters 1 to 4 of the Dhammapada: the twin verses, earnestness, thought and flowers, opened again by a reader who has crossed a few floods since the first time through.
To keep on the shelf: new verses in old pages, waiting for the next reader you become. Two weeks, gathered.
